```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import Markdown
from _lib.orplot import shade_polygon, convex_hull, clip_halfplane, mark_point, COLORS
from _lib.toy_benders import XL, XU, PIECES, X_INT, f, classic_benders, routine1

LOG = classic_benders()
XH, TH = LOG[-1]["x"], LOG[-1]["t"]           # LP optimum where classical Benders stalls
R1 = routine1(XH, TH, split=(1.0, 2.0), init=((0.0, 0.0),))
T_TOP = 10.5
XS = np.linspace(XL, XU, 400)
FX = np.array([f(x) for x in XS])

def piece_polygon(known, side):
    """P_r with only the known cuts: x-range of the term, t >= every known cut."""
    V = [(XL, -0.5), (XU, -0.5), (XU, T_TOP), (XL, T_TOP)]
    V = clip_halfplane(V, (1, 0), 1.0) if side == 0 else clip_halfplane(V, (-1, 0), -2.0)
    for a, g in known:                       # t >= a - g x   <=>   -g x - t <= -a
        V = clip_halfplane(V, (-g, -1), -a)
    return V

def cut_from_alpha(alpha):
    a0, ax, at = alpha                       # a0 + ax x + at t <= 0
    if abs(at) < 1e-9:
        return None
    return (a0 / -at, ax / -at)             # t >= p + q x  ->  return (p, q)
```

## In one paragraph

Classical Benders decomposition [@benders1962] generates cuts from a subproblem that
never sees the integrality of the master variables, so its cuts can at best be tight for
the **continuous** relaxation of the Benders reformulation (see
[Limits of classical Benders cuts](../theory-and-mechanism.qmd#limits)). Fang, Sin and
Byeon combine Benders decomposition with disjunctive programming [@balas1979; @balas1998]
to generate cuts for the **convex hull** of the integer-feasible part instead. Their
routine reuses an existing Benders oracle unchanged. It gives a valid cut even when
stopped early, and for mixed-binary problems it makes the mixed-integer master
unnecessary in theory. Computationally, it shrinks branch-and-bound trees, often by an
order of magnitude on hard instances.

## The problem they address

Using the notation of the [theory page](../theory-and-mechanism.qmd), the Benders
reformulation is $\min\{c^\top x + t : (x, t) \in L,\; x \in X\}$, where $L$ is described
by optimality and feasibility cuts. Any classical oracle — the original one, Pareto-optimal
cuts [@magnanti1981], in-out stabilization [@benameur2007], and so on — returns
hyperplanes separating a point from $L$. The authors' point is that, when
$\mathrm{conv}\big((X \times \mathbb{R}) \cap L\big)$ is much smaller than $L$, no such
cut can close the gap, however good the oracle. They conjecture this is a major
contributor to the tail-off of Benders decomposition.

Their motivating example (their Section 1.2) has an integer set $X$ of $51 \times 2$
points, only two of which are feasible. A Benders implementation with an advanced
oracle, run either as BendersSeq or as BendersBnB, explores more than a quarter of $X$
before proving optimality. The authors note that such structure is not pathological:
Benders reformulations of bilevel problems with convex followers behave similarly.

## Main idea: disjunctive cuts for the Benders reformulation

Take a disjunction that no integer point violates, typically a split
$\phi^\top x \le \phi_0 \lor \phi^\top x \ge \phi_0 + 1$ (see
[What Is Disjunctive Programming?](../../../integer-programming/disjunctive-programming/introduction.qmd)).
Intersecting it with the continuous relaxation gives pieces $P_1, P_2$, and a
**disjunctive cut** is an inequality valid for $\mathrm{conv}(P_1 \cup P_2)$ that cuts
off the current point. Normally such a cut comes from a cut-generating LP over the
pieces, using the [hull formulation](../../../integer-programming/disjunctive-programming/big-m-vs-hull.qmd)
or its dual, the [CGLP](../../../integer-programming/disjunctive-programming/solving.qmd).

The obstacle is that the pieces contain $L$, which is described by **exponentially many
Benders cuts that nobody has generated yet**. The paper's key device makes the
cut-generating problem discover the Benders cuts it needs as it goes.

### The `disjunctiveOracle` (their Routine 1)

The cut-generating problem is written in hull form: one homogenized copy
$(\omega_x^r, \omega_t^r, \omega_0^r)$ of the variables per disjunctive term $r$, glued
together so that their sum equals the point to separate, up to a distance $\tau$ that is
minimized. The routine then repeats:

1. Solve the cut-generating LP using only the Benders cuts known so far, a relaxation
   of $L$.
2. For each term $r$ with weight $\omega_0^r > 0$, **rescale** its copy back to an actual
   point, $(x', t') = (\omega_x^r, \omega_t^r)/\omega_0^r$. This is the
   "[divide by the weight](../../../integer-programming/disjunctive-programming/big-m-vs-hull.qmd#reading-the-hull-formulation-vk-is-lambda_k-times-a-point-of-p_k)"
   step of the hull formulation.
3. Hand $(x', t')$ to an **ordinary, unmodified Benders oracle**. If the oracle finds a
   violated Benders cut, add its homogenized version to the cut-generating LP for every
   term and go back to step 1.
4. When no term is violated, read the disjunctive cut off the dual values.

Their Proposition 3 is what makes step 3 correct: a hyperplane separating the rescaled
point from $L$, once homogenized, separates the scaled copy from the homogenized set
$L^{\#}$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-routine1
#| fig-cap: "Our own run of Routine 1 on the one-dimensional example from the theory page, with the split $x \\le 1 \\lor x \\ge 2$ and the reverse polar normalization with direction $(0,1)$, which lifts the point vertically. To show the discovery step, the routine starts knowing only $t \\ge 0$. Left: with so little known, the point $(\\hat x, \\hat t)$ (red) already lies in the hull of the pieces. The two rescaled points (×) are checked by the ordinary Benders oracle, which finds both violated and returns two Benders cuts. Right: with those cuts, the point must be lifted by $\\tau = 2/3$ to reach the hull. The rescaled points now lie on $f$, so the routine stops and the duals give the disjunctive cut $t \\ge 7 - 2x$ (dashed). In the spirit of Figure 3 of @fang2026."
n = len(R1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n, figsize=(4.4 * n, 4.0), sharey=True)
axes = np.atleast_1d(axes)
for ax, it in zip(axes, R1):
    ax.set_xlim(XL - 0.2, XU + 0.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, T_TOP)
    ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.5, alpha=0.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
    ax.plot(XS, FX, color="black", lw=1.4, label="$f$ (unknown to the routine)")
    P1, P2 = piece_polygon(it["known"], 0), piece_polygon(it["known"], 1)
    shade_polygon(ax, convex_hull(P1 + P2), COLORS["hull"], alpha=0.15, lw=1.0)
    shade_polygon(ax, P1, COLORS["p1"], alpha=0.25)
    shade_polygon(ax, P2, COLORS["p2"], alpha=0.25)
    for c in it["checked"]:
        ax.scatter(c["x"], c["t"], marker="x", s=70, lw=2.2, zorder=7,
                   color=COLORS["weak"] if c["violated"] else COLORS["hull"])
    mark_point(ax, (XH, TH), COLORS["weak"], size=55)
    if it["tau"] > 1e-9:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(XH, TH + it["tau"]), xytext=(XH, TH),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["weak"], lw=1.5))
        p, q = cut_from_alpha(it["alpha"])
        ax.plot(XS, p + q * XS, ls="--", color="black", lw=1.4)
    known = ", ".join("$t\\geq 0$" if g == 0 else f"$t\\geq {a:g}-{g:g}x$".replace("-1x", "-x")
                      for a, g in it["known"])
    ax.set_title(f"Iteration {it['rho'] + 1}: $\\tau = {it['tau']:.3f}$\nknown cuts: {known}",
                 fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_ylabel("$t$")
axes[0].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-routine1
#| tbl-cap: "Our run of Routine 1 on the toy example. Each row is one solve of the cut-generating LP; the rescaled points are checked by the classical Benders oracle."
rows = []
for it in R1:
    pts = "; ".join(f"$({c['x'] + 0.0:.2f},\\,{round(c['t'], 6) + 0.0:.2f})$ {'violated → cut' if c['violated'] else 'in $L$'}"
                    for c in it["checked"])
    cut = cut_from_alpha(it["alpha"])
    cut_s = "—" if (cut is None or it["tau"] < 1e-9) else f"$t \\geq {cut[0]:.0f} {cut[1]:+.0f}x$"
    rows.append(f"| {it['rho'] + 1} | {it['tau']:.3f} | {pts} | {cut_s} |")
Markdown("| Iteration | $\\tau$ | Rescaled points checked by the oracle | Disjunctive cut |\n"
         "|---:|---:|---|---|\n" + "\n".join(rows))
```

On the [theory page](../theory-and-mechanism.qmd#limits) this cut lifts the master's
lower bound from 7.0, the best any Benders cut can do, to 7.5, the integer optimum.

### Properties the authors emphasize

- **Existing oracles are reused as-is.** No integer variables are added to the
  subproblem, and its dual feasible region does not change. Structure-exploiting
  oracles therefore keep working, such as the closed-form, solver-free subproblems
  for facility location of @fischetti2017. The authors stress this as a key difference
  from Lagrangian or extended-formulation approaches.
- **Safe to stop early.** Every intermediate solve of the cut-generating LP yields a
  valid cut that supports a relaxation lying between the convex hull and $L$ (their
  Proposition 4).
- **Free Benders cuts.** The cuts found in step 3 are Benders cuts at automatically
  perturbed points. They can also be added to the master, with an effect similar to
  in-out stabilization [@benameur2007] but without choosing a core point by hand.
- **Higher-rank cuts.** Earlier disjunctive cuts can be included in the cut-generating
  LP, so new cuts build on old ones.
- **Parallelism.** The terms of the disjunction, and separable subproblems such as
  scenarios, can be handled in parallel (their Routine 2).

## Theory

**A unified normalization.** A cut-generating program needs a normalization, otherwise
it is unbounded (see [why](../../../integer-programming/disjunctive-programming/solving.qmd#the-cut-generating-lp)).
The authors write it as a support-function constraint $\sigma_C(\alpha_x) \le 1$ for a
compact convex set $C$. Choosing $C$ as a unit ball recovers norm-based normalization;
choosing $C$ as a single point recovers reverse polar normalization. Their Theorem 1
shows the dual computes a **gauge distance** from the point to the convex hull, which
recovers the known geometric interpretations of both schemes in a single derivation and
gives a recipe for designing new ones. (Our figure uses the single-point case with
$C = \{(0, 1)\}$, which is why the point is lifted vertically.)

**No MILP master for mixed-binary problems.** Using Balas's sequential convexification
[@balas1998], their Algorithm 3 adds one lift-and-project cut [@balas1993] per binary
variable, each time including the cuts found before. Their Theorem 2 shows it terminates
finitely with an optimal solution while only ever solving LPs. In branch-and-bound
terms, the tree could in principle stop at the root. The authors present this as the
first such result that also covers **separable** subproblems. They contrast it with
Lagrangian-cut methods [@zou2019; @rahmaniani2020], which cannot remove the MILP master
when there is more than one scenario because of a Lagrangian duality gap (their
Example 5).

**Mixed-binary refinements.** They carry the classical strengthening of lift-and-project
cuts [@balasjeroslow1980; @balas1993] and the lifting of node cuts to the whole tree into
the Benders setting, as a cheap post-processing of the dual solution. They also propose
an approximate oracle (their Routine 4).

## Experiments (as reported in the paper)

Setup: Julia/JuMP with CPLEX 22.1.1.0, a 4-hour limit, and 7 cores per run, with extra
UFLP runs on Gurobi 13.0.0 in an appendix. The methods compared are the extensive
formulation solved directly (**EXT**), conventional branch-and-Benders-cut (**CBD**),
and their disjunctive version (**DBD**), which calls the disjunctive oracle every 250
fractional nodes on simple splits $x_i \le 0 \lor x_i \ge 1$.

| Problem | What they report |
|---|---|
| Uncapacitated facility location, 250 customers (21 hard instances) | EXT unsolved on 8, CBD unsolved on 1, DBD solved all 21. Relative to EXT, CBD's node count grew by 617.1% on average, DBD's by 74.2%. On the 7 hardest, DBD used 38% of CBD's time and 11.52% of its nodes. |
| Facility location, 500 and 750 customers | EXT hit the limit everywhere. DBD almost always explored fewer nodes and reached better lower bounds than CBD, and solved 3 instances CBD could not. |
| Stochastic network interdiction (456 scenarios, 70 instances) | Easy for CBD (194.41 s on average), so the extra subproblem solves cost more than they save: DBD was 2.30× (snipno3) and 1.81× (snipno4) slower. On the hardest instances, DBD was faster and needed about 10–16% of CBD's nodes. |
| UFLP with Gurobi (appendix) | All methods improved and the CBD–DBD gap narrowed, consistent with Gurobi deriving strong cuts internally, but DBD still won on most instances. |

**Bottom line.** Disjunctive Benders cuts pay off on large, hard instances with big
integrality gaps, where they recover much of the strength of the full formulation
while keeping the speed of decomposition. On easy instances, the extra oracle calls can
cost more than the stronger cuts save.

## Relation to other approaches

The paper compares DBD in detail (their Section 5) with:

- **project-and-cut / cut-and-project split cuts** [@bodur2017], which work with the
  original extended formulation or modified subproblems;
- **Lagrangian cuts** [@zou2019; @rahmaniani2020], which add integrality to the
  subproblem;
- **mixed-integer rounding** of existing Benders cuts [@bodurluedtke2017], which the
  authors see as complementary.

Their stated advantage is scalability. DBD only calls ordinary Benders oracles and
solves a continuous problem whose size can be controlled. The other approaches can win
on problems small enough that their heavier subproblems remain cheap.
